daily_reality.typical_workday: Acupuncturists work a typical 40-hour week, seeing 15-30 patients per week in smaller practices. First-time appointments take ~70 minutes for in-depth health history analysis. Daily tasks: patient intake and health history review, pulse and tongue diagnosis, checking vital signs, inserting acupuncture needles, formulating herbal preparations, applying cups/acupressure/massage, documenting treatment plans and progress notes. Significant time on practice management — scheduling, ordering supplies, billing, insurance claims, and marketing. Most are solo or small-practice owners.
deadlines: Continuing education requirements (typically 60 PDA points per recertification)
daily_reality.seasonality: Seasonal allergy treatment peaks in spring/fall. Pain management demand steady year-round. Holiday stress and seasonal affective disorder increase visits in winter. Fertility/IVF support cycles create treatment clusters. Insurance deductible resets in January drive new patient influx.

laws: State Acupuncture Practice Acts (47 states + DC regulate acupuncture)
Herbal medicine prescribing regulations (varies by state)
Dry needling scope battles with physical therapists
regulatory.licensing: Master's degree (MSAOM/MAOM) or Doctorate (DACM/DAOM) from CCAOM-accredited program. NCCAOM certification required by 22 states, exam used by 26 more. State licensure varies: LAc, Lic.Ac, AP (Florida), CA. 47 states + DC regulate acupuncture; Alabama, Oklahoma, South Dakota do not. NCCAOM recertification every 4 years with 60 PDA points. 3 states have no regulation for acupuncturists.
regulatory.penalties: Practicing without license: fines and potential criminal charges. State board investigations from patient complaints. License suspension/revocation for violations. Malpractice liability for needle injuries or adverse reactions. Clean needle technique violations. Herbal medicine adverse events liability.

career_psychology.burnout: Burnout driven by juggling clinical practice with business management responsibilities. Financial stress from lower patient volumes and insurance challenges. Smaller practices (15-30 patients/week) create pressure on revenue. Alternative practitioners often feel uncomfortable with business/marketing. Patient expectations for quick fixes vs reality of TCM's gradual approach causes frustration. Physical demands of standing and performing treatments all day contribute to fatigue.
